author: Malik Miah, Barry Sheppard
title: United States: Trump and Republicans routed in mid-term elections
content:
The Democratic Party won sweeping victories in the United States midterm elections on November 3, in a dramatic refutation of President Donald Trump and the Republican Party he controls.

These results were not a vote of confidence in the Democrats but were a rejection of Trump and Trumpism. The majority of US voters do not trust either party.

Going into the elections, Republicans held small minorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

All 435 members of the House are elected every two years and the Democrats won a decisive majority of 254-256 seats with a few results still to be finalised at the time of writing.

One-third of the 100-seat Senate is elected every two years for a six-year term and the Democrats now hold a majority of 54-56 seats.

This is the biggest change in Congressional seats since 1974, when the Democrats swept to victory and Republican President Richard Nixon was driven out of office, in a scandal resulting from him sending thugs into the Democratic Party headquarters.

The Democrats also made sweeping gains in state and local elections.

In Texas, considered a Republican stronghold, Democratic candidate and Mexican American Gina Hinojosa was elected governor — the first Latinx elected to this office in any state.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim ever elected to the Senate, despite facing a virulent Islamophobic campaign against him, where Trump called him a “terrorist”.

Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first African American woman elected as governor in Georgia, in the nation’s “deep South”.

Native American Deb Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico and Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American elected to the Senate.

The first openly gay Senate candidate, Chris Pappas, was elected in New Hampshire.

In Mississippi, African American Senate candidate Scott Colom leads by a narrow margin in a race too close to call, and in Alaska, Native American Mary Peltola has a slight lead in the race for the Senate.

Eight candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) were elected to Congress, including Chris Rabb (Pennsylvania), Rashida Tlaib and Donavan McKinney (Minnesota), Melat Kiros (Colorado), Angela Gonzales-Torres (California), Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York).

DSA candidate Nithya Raman won the race for Mayor of Los Angeles, Janeese Lewis George won the mayoral race in Washington DC and Claudia Jimenez in East Bay, California.

The DSA grew rapidly following Donald Trump’s election in 2016 and on the wave of support for self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders — who is not a member of DSA. DSA seeks to strengthen the progressive wing of the Democrats and is criticised by the revolutionary left for advocating progressive reforms within the capitalist system, rather than its overthrow. Nevertheless, Trump labels DSA and left Democrats as “communist” and the Democratic Party as “socialist”.

A large turnout from young people eager for progressive change, and from the Black and Latinx communities were key to the Republican defeat.

Black community organisers led in Southern states. They made it clear they were making the elections an act of defending Black people from the Republican drive to go back to “Jim Crow-type” oppression in the South.

There is no mass (even mini-mass) working class electoral party, or parties of the oppressed nationalities in the US and the Green Party is weak. So there is no other choice in elections than between two capitalist parties, and results have to be analysed in that reality.

Some of the main factors for the anti-Republican vote include that the Trump administration is the most corrupt in US history. Add to that the Iran war, Trump’s cruel anti-immigration policy against Latinx communities, and Trump’s tariffs on imports that have driven up inflation, outpacing wage rises and impacting living standards and affordability.

At the same time, Trump and his billionaire friends have gotten richer, as have millionaires and capitalists in general. Trump has increased his own wealth by more than $3 billion and his immediate family by another $3 billion, since he took office in 2025.

Trump’s tariffs have cost working class families, on average, a minimum of $1000 — which continues to rise.

Trump’s war on Iran has made the price of petrol and diesel skyrocket. Farmers, whose equipment largely runs on diesel, turned against Trump and voted against him.

The cruelty of masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents grabbing people who have brown skin and herding them — including little children — into mass, inhumane detention centres is a factor in why more Latinx candidates were elected to Congress, making the Latinx caucus the largest ever.

Trump doesn’t hate all immigrants. If they are white, especially white racist South Africans like Elon Musk, they are especially welcome.

Trump labels other African countries as “shit holes” and won’t issue visas to their citizens. He has singled out Somali populations in Minnesota and other states for ICE assaults, even threatening to deport Ilan Omar, a Somali Congressional Representative from Minneapolis.

The civil rights commission of his Department of Justice doesn’t defend people of colour (the real population suffering discrimination), but pursues cases of alleged discrimination of whites because of programs to further diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI). Trump has outlawed DEI by fiat.

What will the Democrats do when the new Congress takes office in January? What will they really change?

Will they end Trump’s unilateral war against Iran or will they demand Iran agree to violations of its sovereignty and submit to US (and Israeli) domination? Will they reinstate DEI? Will they champion the interests of working people? Unlikely.

It remains to be seen just what they will do.

Trump’s response to the election was to appoint Stephen Miller — the openly white nationalist bigot and architect of Trump’s racist campaign against immigrants — as his new chief of staff.

This indicates Trump is going to double down on his anti-immigration policies and racist targeting of Latinx communities, unleashing ICE and Border Force agents against them. He will also likely confront the Democrat-controlled Congress and veto any (even mildly) progressive laws it passes.

author: Coral Wynter
title: Standing with the women and girls of Afghanistan
content:
About 110 people from Australia and Britain joined Amnesty International (AI) in an on-line forum, on September 23, to hear about the human rights group's strategy to support women in Afghanistan. Kathy Allan from AI introduced the forum by saying that when Kabul fell on August 15, 2021, the United States handed over power to the Taliban, after the US Coalition, including Australian forces, had carried out a military intervention into Afghanistan for two decades.

The Taliban has 164 decrees targeting women and girls. Women have been barred from most jobs, and from working with non-government organisations (NGOs). Girls are banned from secondary school and university, parks, gyms and beauty salons. Women cannot speak publicly. LGBTIQ+ Afghans have been forced into hiding.

The Taliban is also attacking ethnic and religious minorities, as well as journalists and human rights defenders.

This institutionalised pattern of systemic domination and oppression based on gender has been labelled “gender apartheid”. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to impose this extreme form of gender discrimination.

Right now, international law has no statute that fully captures this situation. AI is calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime under international law.

Muslima, an Afghan educator and writer, told the forum, “Almost overnight, the door to our classroom was closed. Just because you were a girl, you lost your classroom.

“I never imagined that my future would just mean I stay home ... simply because I was born a girl. Being at home every day felt like a prison, like being in jail. Where do I go? My human rights were wiped out.

“But now I have a computer, my classroom to the outside world. All that I have is a small screen in my room. If they find out, I can face charges.

“Thousands of girls have no access to a computer and internet, but I am lucky. Afghan women can’t talk about their stories, nor can they speak about these issues. Girls of 12 years of age are denied the simple right to education, to learn, to develop their skills, to make friends.

“The Taliban can’t build a strong future by excluding half of the population. Afghanistan is losing enormous [human] potential.

“I want the world to see something beyond our suffering. Women are still writing, working, advocating, creating, contributing and building. If you want to support Afghan women, you must listen to them.

“When the headlines disappear, Afghan women do not disappear.

“So my message is clear: make a space for us to speak. Share our voices.

“Sometimes solidarity begins with something as simple as a refusal to forget. Listen to the voices of Afghan women, who are denied their human rights,” Muslima concluded.

The next speaker was Shaharzad Akbar, a human rights activist from Afghanistan, currently living in exile. She talked about the Peoples Tribunal on Women of Afghanistan, which was held in Madrid, Spain, in October last year and hosted by four Afghan women’s organisations.

They are worried that the actions of the Taliban, as the de facto regime, are being normalised in the region. The Taliban currently have consulates in Germany, China, India and Turkiye, although only Russia officially recognises the Taliban government. Europe is now holding conversations with the Taliban regarding potentially deporting Afghan men and women.

Akbar said, “Women are not able to train as midwives or doctors ... Women will die from preventable diseases because there are not enough female health-care providers.”

Women are suffering from domestic abuse, but it is not considered a crime inside Afghanistan. Emotional, economic and physical abuses are not criminalised. Husbands are allowed by law to punish their wives for any offence.

Women can only go to a judge to make a complaint if they have obvious bruises or broken bones — and face many hurdles to do so. They are not allowed to leave the house alone and a male family member has to accompany them to the court. So a brother or father has to be convinced to support them.

The woman has to relay her message to the judge through a man. If she is believed and she has broken bones caused by her husband, he will be imprisoned for 15 days. He usually returns home only to repeat the abuse.

“We have had increased killing of women, increased suicides of women and a mental health crisis for women and girls in Afghanistan. They don’t see a future for themselves. They are imprisoned in their homes, suffering abuse and forced into early marriages. Despite all this, the Taliban are being normalised.

“We thought if we held a tribunal, where people could hear what is happening, we could slow down this normalisation process. Do we really want our governments to engage with a regime like this?

“Some 24 survivors, some who were refugees, spoke to the Tribunal by audio or written testimonies, for they feared for their own lives and that of their families.”

In December, a panel of eight judges declared that non-normalisation of the Taliban should occur. “So you should watch very carefully what the Australian government is doing in regards to their relationship to the Taliban,” said Akbar.

Two years ago, in September 2024, Australia, Germany, The Netherlands and Canada promised to hold Afghanistan and the Taliban accountable for violations of the Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW). Afghanistan is a signatory to CEDAW. The countries said that if they didn’t get a satisfactory answer, they would take the Afghan government to the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

Afghani women have been asking these four countries each month when they are going to take the Taliban to the ICJ. “We receive vague answers. So please ask your government what happened to the CEDAW legal initiative?

“I know it won’t solve our problems but it will tell the women and girls of Afghanistan that the world stands with them. We need to tell the world to channel aid to Afghan women and force the Taliban to reverse the codification of gender apartheid,” concluded Akbar.

Azadah Raz Mohammad, one of the prosecutors who appeared before the Peoples Tribunal, and legal advisor to the campaign to end gender apartheid, told the forum: “The current objective is to codify gender apartheid under the current treaty we have before the UN, the crimes against humanity treaty.”

The phrase “gender apartheid” was first used in the period 1996 to 2001, when the Taliban was in power for the first time.

“We now have 14 states that have expressed support for codification of gender apartheid and seven states that have submitted formal proposals to the UN committee for inclusion of the practice in the crimes against humanity. These states include Australia, Timor-Leste, Luxembourg, Iceland, the former government of Afghanistan and Uruguay. This will go for negotiation to the UN in 2028.”

The final speaker, Fatima Frotan, is doing grassroots work with Afghan women in communities, including distributing menstruation pads in Daikundi and Uruzgan provinces, through personal contacts.

Frotan said men and boys in Afghanistan are getting educated in religious idolatry and misogyny and there has been a rise in the establishment of madrasas across the country by the Taliban.

Frotan was part of an organisation called Afghans for Progressive Thinking.

“We began talking to a number of youth. We started a pilot program for women and girls in Kabul. Afghanistan is a deeply religious country, and Islam is a big part of their identity. We introduced them to a more egalitarian interpretation of Islam, where they could find the agency and empowerment within their own identity, which was quite successful.

“In the western part of Kabul there have been targeted attacks on the Hazara neighbourhoods. Shiite education facilities have been taken over by the Taliban. LGBTQIA people are persecuted.

“We have to stop the campaign of genocide against Hazara peoples and other minorities. We want the West to expand the number of scholarships given to Afghani women and to expand the number of scholarships to overseas universities, and to help with the visas, especially for women at risk,” she said.

Amnesty International's 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, from November 25 to December 10, is focussed on pressuring the Australian government to use its diplomatic influence to support recognition of gender apartheid under international law and follow through on accountability for the Taliban’s crimes against women and girls.

[For more information, visit: amnesty.org.au.]

author: Mazin Qumsiyeh
title: Palestinian ecologist tells COP31: ‘Peace is an environmental necessity’
content:
Mazin Qumsiyeh, from the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability at Bethlehem University, delivered this speech to an ancillary meeting organised at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) being held in Türkiye.

We cannot seriously address the climate crisis while ignoring war, militarism, occupation, and the enormous environmental costs of colonisation.

Here in Palestine, the colonial genocide and ethnic cleansing of our people since 1948 has resulted in half a million killed, and now 8.5 million displaced or refugees.

We are working now to get the United Nations to pass an ecocide convention similar to the genocide convention.

The ecocide is global problem and goes beyond borders.

There is no other area where more bombs were dropped relative to population size than Western Asia.

The ecocide is more than just war effect and it does go beyond borders. The Zionist drying up of the Jordan River basin affects four countries; the uprooting of millions of trees and the pollution from the war on the people of Gaza is spreading along the Mediterranean coastline resulting affecting habitats and people.

War is also a climate issue as military activities consume enormous quantities of fossil fuels, destroy infrastructure, generate toxic pollution and release greenhouse gases.

These are often poorly reported or excluded from national climate accounting.

The destruction of Gaza has generated enormous greenhouse gas emissions, both directly through military operations and indirectly through the destruction and future reconstruction of buildings and infrastructure.

A study published in March reported that 33.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO₂) equivalent had been produced in the destruction of Gaza — a tiny area of 365 square kilometres.

This conservative figure does not take into account the destroyed trees (we studied those by remote sensing), nor the jet fuel burned in countless United States/Israeli sorties to bomb Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Iran.

The 2026 One Earth study estimated that US deliveries of military equipment to Israel between October 2023 and January 2025 involved approximately 50,000 tonnes of supplies transported through 507 aircraft and 107 ship journeys.

The US, which remains the largest single cause of climate change emissions — and it is exempted from reporting on these, has nearly depleted its stockpile of missiles via deliveries to Israel.

Military infrastructure, walls, fortifications and security installations also require enormous quantities of concrete, steel and energy.

The long-term environmental costs is catastrophic: Contaminated soil and water, destruction of agricultural land, damaged wastewater systems, loss of vegetation and even more people dying from diseases and deprivation than those killed directly by these weapons.

More studies and public attention are needed on all of this.

The destruction of ecosystems, like has happened in Palestine, makes communities less resilient to climate change.

Destruction of trees, agricultural land and natural vegetation reduces carbon storage. Soil degradation reduces water infiltration and groundwater recharge.

The destruction of wetlands and natural habitats undermines biodiversity and ecosystem services. Damage to water, sewage and electricity infrastructure increases pollution and dependence on burning wood and diesel for fuel.

The destruction of agricultural systems undermines food sovereignty and increases dependence on imported food.

The UN Environment Program’s September 2025 assessment provides particularly disturbing evidence. By May 2025, 97.1% of tree crops and 82.4% of annual crops in Gaza had been damaged. Approximately 61 million tonnes of debris would require management.

Climate justice requires accountability, not selective accounting.

There is a fundamental contradiction in international climate policy. Governments demand carbon reductions from ordinary citizens, farmers and industries, while military emissions remain inadequately accounted for.

The Paris Agreement climate framework does not impose a comprehensive mandatory reporting system for military emissions. Thus we demand mandatory, transparent reporting of military greenhouse gas emissions, including arms production, military logistics, combat operations and reconstruction.

We often speak about saving the planet for future generations.

But what does that mean to a Palestinian child growing up in Gaza, whose home, school, agricultural land, water resources and natural environment have been destroyed?

What does climate justice mean when billions are spent on weapons while communities struggle for clean water, food and the basic conditions for life? We cannot separate the climate crisis from militarism, colonialism and the unequal distribution of power.

We cannot talk about sustainability while financing destruction.

We, the ordinary citizens, have the burden of responsibility not only to report this climate abuse but offer alternatives.

Our Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability provides practical on-the-ground community-led models for peace building, mitigation, adaptation, reduction and much more.

Our vision is sustainable human and natural communities and our motto is respect: For ourselves — empowerment — for other people and for mother nature.

Peace is an environmental necessity. Justice is a prerequisite for sustainability. Protecting nature means protecting the right of people to live in dignity, freedom and harmony with their environment.

[To follow Mazin Qumsiyeh, from the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability at Bethlehem University, visit his blog Popular Resistance.]

Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability

author: Tamara Pearson
title: Journalism and news in times of catastrophe and enshittification
content:
I pace my small apartment for almost an hour after interviewing a fellow journalist in Mexico who was kidnapped by organised crime groups. Another day, a source has been arrested, another dies in a suspicious car accident. Others tell compelling stories of saving rivers and stopping powerful corporations. I feel alive when I work. But often also worried, deeply sad, and overlooked.

I also work as a global features editor, and the news comes in throughout the day, announcing more horrific events. Another oil spill, more destruction of the environment, of cultures, of people's youths and their futures.

Committed with such impunity, it sometimes leaves me questioning the impact of my work. The repetitive and ongoing nature of such injustices can also make journalism feel routine and close to pointless.

These are tough times for people reading or listening to the news, and for those real journalists who challenge economic and political power rather than aligning with it. But we must continue to stay informed—ignoring the bad news won't stop it.

Courageous journalism is needed more than ever, but it is being smothered by online platforms. Social media, search engines, and the web are increasingly enshitified—inundated with advertising, incorrect information, AI delusions, and mundane, vacuous viral videos.

It is an information crisis and a justice crisis all at once. But just as excessive consumerism and the approximately 48,000 overflowing landfills across the world are a clear call to only use what we need, these crises also embody within them a call for deep change, for a reckoning.

AI dominance begs us to return to everything that is humanising, creative, and real. Injustice and the climate crisis call for structural action and a strengthening of good journalism. The mainstream outlets beholden to corporations and in denial of empire and inequality are increasingly and obviously, useless.

Media outlets and other sources of information, like search engines and social media, are skewing perceptions about what matters. The amount of attention and space given to different regions, issues, and people forges a hierarchy of concerns.

Issues covered tediously can risk desensitising, normalising,and numbing. But overlooked news and silence numbs in malevolent and long-lasting ways, infusing populations with extremely high levels of tolerance and deflection.

Mass hunger in a world that produces an excess of food is a raging nightmare, deserving of daily coverage and strike action until it ends. Yet most people are accustomed.

For the journalists and outlets with integrity, at times it can feel like there is nothing left to say; that we've reported the injustices over and over. That all we are doing is documenting how the house is falling apart. This is indicative of a need to take things to the next level.

So how do we do good journalism, when everything is at stake and none of the polluting and warring criminals are held accountable? How can our news reading and news producing be useful, even as long-term worry exhausts us and narrows cognitive flexibility and creativity? How do we ensure clarity and care, without also falling apart?

The algorithmic boosting of low-grade and commercial content, accompanies the burying of critical insight and investigation. Amid catastrophe, injustice, and repression, the key sources of information — rather than enlightening — are calculated to numb and dull people.

The social media, information, book, and media landscapes are rapidly deteriorating as ad load is growing to ridiculous amounts. Every other post is sponsored content or online recipes. Many articles are unreadable without a browser or tools that remove all the ads. Our feeds are industrial swamplands of sponsored content and viral AI videos and stories. And for some demographics, objectified images of women.

Even newsletter spaces like Substack boost existing privilege (almost all the top newsletters are by men) and seek profitability. Meanwhile AI search engine summaries are discouraging direct reads of alternative media outlets. First page search results are likewise dominated by corporations like Expedia, United States outlets (even for users who aren't there), and mediocre click-bait websites. It's hard to compete, and our in-depth reporting can feel like feeble feathers in a hurricane.

Further, people expect shorter and short content. Two minute videos are now too long. Scrolling and short formats promote habits and standards that reject complexity, discomfort, intention, depth, process, and contemplation, and instead—especially when combined with e-consumerism—a desire for instant results is fostered.

Algorithmic curation and content recommendation based on predicted interests is understandably tempting for people who are overworked and exhausted. Intentional decision making is a mental load after a long day of work, caring for others, dealing with bureaucracy or discrimination, or working through trauma.

But being selective about news, information, and entertainment is practically a radical act amid such a deluge of crap and with companies like Meta supporting the right and suppressing alternatives and resistance (for example the restrictions Meta placed on Lula’s accounts during the Brazilian elections).

Intentionality is particularly necessary for international news, where regions like Latin America, Africa, and Asia have to wrestle for relevance in a rigid hierarchy of life that ranks them lower. Injustice here must be hundreds of times worse to capture interest. Indigenous towns drone bombed and eliminated aren't interesting enough. The recent gold mine collapses in Sudan and the millions forcibly displaced there, barely register.

Readers and reporters can gain back some control over their local and international news consumption with scheduled news time and short lists of strong pro-people, pro-planet media outlets and newsletters like mine, Excluded Headlines, which seek to re-balance world news coverage.

Well-written or produced news is actually good for us. It orders the chaos and gives it meaning. Depth and clarity around the causes and forces behind the horror is important for knowing how to put out the fire, as well as for our own well being and for informing our collective decision making.

Good journalism also restores a sense of freedom and relief after all the enshittification. It reminds us that not everything is garbage.

Avoiding the bad news won't help with handling reality. But the type of awareness matters, and a profound awareness of global and local forces is important for countering isolation, and for experiencing the patterns as history takes place that reveal connectedness between issues, resistance, and events, and for never falling into the trap of tolerating harm.

On the other hand, the banking system of education, AI, and low-quality media, by fostering an inability to think critically and under-representing oppressed peoples, can strengthen systemic class, race and nationality, gender, sexuality, and disability violence.

Hence, media and information isn't a side note to life, it is decisive. And the best journalism isn't done from the sidelines, but from the battlegrounds and fields.

Parachuting into another country or into an issue to cover them doesn't work. Reporting from a couch or a mansion, from the pinnacles of privilege, and from the corporate headquarters of empires isn't journalism.

We need reality — raw, and decoded.

Not greenwashing, not whitewashing, not spinning away the injustice, sugar-coating disregard and cruelty, justifying the intolerable. Not the naive glorifying of right-wing forces in Global South countries, or platitudes of balance and neutrality from outlets very much aligned with corporations and Euro or US-centric and pro-war perspectives.

Interestingly, despite the glut, most people (86% globally) do recognise climate change as serious, for example. And that is where the hope is. About 56% of people think about climate change on a daily or weekly basis, and a poll of ten European countries found 77% of respondents believe that companies should be held responsible for environmental harm.

The difficult next step is facing up to the fact that protecting the environment and building true global equality and justice involve some discomfort and uncertainty. Tweaking shower times and donating to charities won't cut it. Ending societal and structural addictions to petroleum involves effort, confrontation, and deep change.

Amid the oil spills and bombs, it can be hard to dream. Here in central Mexico, organised crime controls streets and transport, as well as extorting, forcibly disappearing, and tainting the air with tension and fear.

It feels close to impossible to imagine building some kind of nurturing community on these bruised and sunken streets. Yet we have to. We have to conjure up hope from the fish-scale-clogged drains and the potholes of life.

We have to free our imaginations from the bare and boring rooms of AI and 3am social media scrolling so we can remember the kite sky parties, the marigold fields, the precious art galleries in Havana overlooking the bay, the rainbow beetles and stealth caterpillars and mulberry silkworms that turn saliva into silk. Like magic.

We're magical too, but we often forget it. Our ability to turn the ordinary into the extraordinary is there, if dusty and atrophied.

I asked a few activists here if I should write another novel. "Is there any point?" I said, discouraged. Things feel too urgent for novels and stories and art. It is a time for strikes, roadblocks, shutting down and building anew. But they said yes, and of course one can do both.

"The harder times are, the more necessary art and creativity is. It provides hope, it keeps us humanised and sensitive to others," replied one friend. So, I've started writing another novel and it is pouring out of me. It will be the messy story of how people do away with borders, global inequality, environmental pillaging, and empire and build something more caring and nurturing than this selfish nightmare.

The AI boom is asking us what it means to be human. That question about our collective identity couldn't have come at a better time. We should refuse AI—not because technology is bad (it isn't) but because of who owns it and how they have looted our intellectual work to control what we know and how we think.

Build shields against the devaluing of life, of our work, of creativity. Turn AI off in search engines or use operators like -AI in searches (and other operators like site:.co to force results from a particular country rather than almost exclusively the US). Boycott corporate media and use search engines that are more neutral than Chrome like Mojeek (less big business but still very Eurocentric), Brave, and Qwant.

AI and billionaire-controlled social media, through the proliferation of so much AI-generated content and unverified or incorrect information, are planting distrust and disillusionment. I mentioned this to my friend.

“Exactly. AI takes away critical thought and dehumanises, and technology is inundating us so we don't feel the loss. When we're overstimulated, we don't pay attention to anything,” she said.

Our attention is everything right now. It is accountability and it is priorities. The news is hard to read, but don't stop. Just be strategic and selective. Let it connect and ground us, and inspire us.

There is so much bravery, beauty, kindness—and therefore such potential. Some media outlets will overlook that, others will highlight the resistances and generosity.

[Tamara Pearson is an Australian-Mexican journalist, editor, activist and literary fiction author living in Puebla, Mexico. Her latest novel is The Eyes of the Earth, and she writes the Global South newsletter Excluded Headlines.]

author: Cas Smith
title: Doctor says Israeli cluster bombs, with Australian tungsten, are targetting Palestinian children
content:
Dr Farah Abdul Aziz, Perth-based general and breast surgeon, volunteered twice in Gaza, including a harrowing period of service in the enclave’s “red zone” from December 2024 to January 2025.

Aziz told Green Left that working in the north of Gaza was “just awful”.

“There were just continuous attacks across the zone from sundown to sunrise, and even during the day. Medical staff could not go out of the hospital at all, because we could easily get bombed at any time.”

Aziz, a member of Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA), was largely tasked with treating head, abdominal and chest injuries.

“The patients I received were the ones who had just survived the blasts that we were hearing all night. It was usually multiple shrapnel injuries, but they were still alive. Then, during the day, it would be single-shot bullet injuries.

“Because I’m not a neurosurgeon, I didn’t treat children who had received a single shot to the head, but I still saw them when my colleagues received them.

“Some had received a single shot to the abdomen or chest; these are little children, you can imagine snipers sniping them from two, three hundred meters away.”

The October protest against the Land Forces weapons expo in Perth condemned Australian governments for embracing the weapons industry and their involvement in supply chains connected to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

author: Sue Bolton, Sarah Hathway
title: Why you should vote Socialist Alliance in Victoria
content:
However, the Liberal-National Coalition and One Nation want to push politics to the right.

The Liberals have overcome years of destructive infighting under the leadership of youthful “clean-skin” Jess Wilson, who the mainstream media is championing.

At the time of writing, the Coalition is leading Labor by about 8% points in polls.

Unsurprisingly, Wilson’s policies do not favour the working class that is doing it tough in Victoria.

The Coalition is promising to “save” $22 billion, over 10 years, by freezing new public sector appointments and it wants to “save” $1 billion by scrapping Victoria’s Treaty with First Nations people.

Wilson has also promised more draconian anti-protest laws by expanding police “move-on” powers, and introducing a bureaucratic permit and registration system for public protests.

These regressive policies aimed at the public sector and the suppression of free speech are being supported by the opportunistic and reactionary One Nation, now polling only 1% point behind Labor.

The Coalition is preferencing One Nation, which wants similar outcomes.

Labor has paved the way for its own defeat by not addressing the cost-of-living crisis, chronic housing stress or a deteriorating public sector — especially in health, education and public transport.

Workers are right to be disillusioned as Victorian Labor has fought against substantive wage rises for public sector workers. It has joined the federal government’s full-frontal attack on the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union, including by calling a royal commission.

The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria is doing huge damage to Labor’s standing, while also destroying the country’ most militant union.

Socialist Alliance does not want the Liberal-National Coalition to win government, with support from One Nation, which purports to be anti-establishment but accepts hand-outs and policy advice from billionaires and bosses.

But Labor’s refusal to push back against the corporations and the billionaires makes this outcome more likely.

That is why it is important to cast your vote for socialists and Greens at this election.

The right has no solutions: Capitalism is creating more endless wars, which then exacerbate cost-of-living rises, including petrol. It is responsible for the climate crisis and consequent extreme weather patterns, which include devastating floods and fires.

Socialist Alliance is running under the slogan: “Fighting for people NOT the billionaires”.

Our anti-capitalist message is aimed at workers who are dissatisfied with Labor. Voting for hypocrites and racists, like One Nation, will not help lower housing prices or pay the grocery and education bills.

Socialist Alliance believes that elections are an opportunity to build support for socialist ideas among the working class and to push back against the hate-driven divide-and-rule policies of the capitalist parties.

We believe we have a unique contribution to make; we are a democratic, non-sectarian party which is focused on building the necessary alliances and mass mobilisations that involve workers in creating the progressive changes we need.

Our election campaign is an extension of this movement-building work we do on a daily basis. Our electoral work is part of our overall goal of creating a party which has as its goal the transformation of society so that it is geared to meet people’s needs.

author: Kerry Smith
title: Solidarity shown to climate action group Rising Tide
content:
Many community-based groups are showing their support for climate action group Rising Tide, which is battling NSW Labor, Newcastle City Council and NSW Police to organise a peaceful protest on Newcastle Harbour, the world’s biggest coal port, on November 14.

You can register for the Paddle for the Planet here, and sign the petition to reverse Newcastle Council's ban on Rising Tide events here.

Below are some of the solidarity statements.

Sydney Students for Climate stands with Rising Tide against the outrageous decision by the City of Newcastle to permanently ban climate protests from council-owned land.

The undemocratic attack on protest rights was passed by the mayor’s deciding vote, after a 6–6 split at the November 10 council meeting. The motion could effectively ban all protests on Newcastle council land.

It was supported by NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns, who wrote a letter endorsing the motion.

Minns has consistently tried to shut down peaceful protests for climate, Palestine and other issues.

We also note that NSW Police are taking Rising Tide to the Supreme Court to try and shut down the November 14 paddle out for the planet.

With the climate hurtling towards disaster and NSW Labor continuing to approve new coal and gas projects, we will fight these anti-protest restrictions and continue demanding action for a safe climate.

SSFC will be at the Paddle for the Planet this Saturday, and the People’s Blockade of the World’s Largest Coal Port in February, and we encourage all to join us.

Socialist Alliance stands with Rising Tide and all groups protesting against the expansion of coal and gas, and for funding a just transition for fossil fuel workers in Muloobinba/Newcastle.

The City of Newcastle’s decision on November 10 to ban Rising Tide, and other groups, from protesting on “community-owned land” is draconian and dangerous.

The motion — adopted by a the independent Mayor’s casting vote — represents yet another attack on citizen’s democratic right to protest in NSW. Three Labor councillors did not support the Mayoral minute, only given half an hour before the meeting, but one did.

While the motion singled out Rising Tide, it said “affiliate groups” were also banned from protesting on council land. When pressed, Mayor Gavin Morris confirmed he also wanted to stop protests that support Palestine.

NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns’ record on trying to stop peaceful protests — on Palestine and for a safe climate — shows just how dangerous he is.

For three years Minns has tried to stop citizens from protesting the genocide in Gaza. He has been spectacularly unsuccessful because he has been challenged, and the courts, including the Supreme Court, have ruled against his efforts to stop people from mobilising together to express their view — the Sydney Harbour Bridge march for humanity being the most prominent example.

Minns is a big fan of coal, and he is now trying to introduce a new law to circumvent a High Court decision stating that NSW planning must take all emissions into account.

Minns has wanted to stop Rising Tide’s peaceful protests for a safe climate at the Newcastle Harbour. For several years he has been pushed back.

Newcastle City Council’s decision to prevent Rising Tide from using foreshore land now and into the future will not deter climate activists.

The NSW Police has lodged an objection in the Supreme Court to also disallow the Rising Tide protest on November 14.

But climate activists will continue to protest NSW Labor’s addiction to fossil fuels, which includes expanding coal mines in the Hunter Valley in a climate crisis.

As COP31 begins in Turkey, Rising Tide is seeking to draw attention to Australia’s complicity in fueling dangerous climate change. Minns is also complicit.

Socialist Alliance has long supported Rising Tide and will be joining the family-friendly flotilla protest at the world’s largest coal port on November 14 at 10am.

City of Sydney for Palestine stands with Rising Tide. Rising Tide has supported and facilitated our actions, and many of our members have volunteered with and participated in actions facilitated by Rising Tide. We know firsthand the power of coming together across movements.

Newcastle Council’s decision to prevent Rising Tide from using council-owned community land for protest events is an attack on the right to protest. We call on the council to reverse it.

From climate justice to Palestinian liberation, our movements depend on the freedom to organise, speak out and take collective action.

Stand with Rising Tide. Defend the right to protest.

The Greens have condemned Newcastle City Council's extraordinary decision to prohibit Rising Tide from using community-owned land for future climate protests, as NSW Police take the peaceful climate movement to the Supreme Court and the Minns Labor Government moves to pass special legislation protecting the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine.

Greens MP and spokesperson for the environment and climate change Sue Higginson said the coordinated political and legal pressure against climate protesters was an alarming escalation in Labor's efforts to protect the coal industry from public scrutiny and opposition.

Greens Leader Senator David Shoebridge said:

“Labor is taking its orders directly from the coal industry, again.

“This decision shows the extent of fossil fuel capture of the Labor party all the way from Local Councils to Federal Parliament.

“These protests were working and that is exactly why the fossil fuel industry got their people in the Liberal and Labor parties to try and ban them.

“While Anthony Albanese is in Türkiye at COP31 talking big on Australia's climate ambitions at home they are blocking protest, approving coal and gas projects and taking the fossil fuel industry’s cash."

“Labor wants applause at COP for its climate leadership while it keeps approving new coal and gas, including a decades‑long extension of the North West Shelf, and that double game is exactly why thousands of people keep turning up in Newcastle every year.

“Labor listens to the money and works alongside the polluters, the Greens listen to the people and work alongside them in our fight for a safe future, because that’s what’s at stake here.”

NSW Greens MP, solicitor, and spokesperson for Climate Change Sue Higginson said:

“NSW Labor has completely lost its way. While the climate crisis accelerates and Australia is leading global climate negotiations at COP31, the Minns Government is rewriting climate laws for coal corporations in violation of the High Court, taking peaceful protesters to court (again) and supporting a Newcastle Council decision to exclude climate campaigners from public land.

“The people of Newcastle and NSW have every right to peacefully protest the ongoing expansion of coal mining and exports through their city. That right belongs to the community, and it cannot be extinguished because Minns and a select few Labor politicians find the message inconvenient.

“Newcastle is home to the world's largest coal export port, and the people who live there are on the front line of the climate crisis. Rising Tide has brought thousands of people together to demand action on coal, and Labor's response is to try to shut them down.

“Three Labor Newcastle councillors stood with the Greens to defend the right to protest, but their colleague, Premier Chris Minns’ minion, with the deciding vote chose to impose an extraordinary and indefinite exclusion on Rising Tide. This is a disgraceful decision that will stand as a historic mistake.

“At the same time, NSW Police are in the Supreme Court trying to prohibit a peaceful flotilla protest from going ahead in the latest attack on legitimate and peaceful democratic activity. Rising Tide has made clear that Saturday's event is intended to be a peaceful, fun gathering to highlight COP31, and the police should be facilitating that democratic expression rather than fighting it in court.

“The Minns Government’s rushing of special legislation through Parliament to protect the billion-dollar Mount Pleasant coal operation from the consequences of a landmark climate law decision is about as egregious as it gets. Labor is prepared to change the law for coal corporations while making it harder and harder for ordinary people to exercise their democratic rights.

“These decisions expose just how deeply the coal industry has embedded itself in the political priorities of NSW Labor. Coal corporations have extraordinary access to government, while the communities demanding a safe climate are met with police, courts and political exclusion.

“The Greens stand with Rising Tide and everyone exercising their right to peaceful protest. Newcastle Council should reverse this decision, NSW Police should safely facilitate Saturday's assembly, and the Minns Government must abandon its special protection for the Mount Pleasant coal mine. Anything less is a deep betrayal of our community and climate.

The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN) condemns Newcastle Council’s decision to ban Rising Tide and associated or affiliated groups, including Palestinian solidarity groups, from holding protests and events on council land.

Peaceful protest is not a privilege granted by politicians or local councils. It is a fundamental democratic right.

We call on Newcastle Council to immediately reverse this decision and on the NSW Government to uphold the right to peaceful assembly, rather than support measures that restrict it.

APAN stands in solidarity with Rising Tide and all communities whose fundamental democratic freedoms are threatened by this decision.

Hiba Farra, APAN Vice President said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to democracy.

“Public spaces belong to the community, not just those whose views are acceptable to governments. First they try to silence Palestinians speaking out against genocide. Now they’re shutting down climate protesters.

“This is not about public safety. It is about silencing dissent and deciding whose voices are allowed to be heard.

“This sweeping restriction sets a dangerous precedent for the right to peaceful protest in NSW, extending beyond climate activism to threaten the ability of Palestinians and their supporters to organise, assemble and demand justice.

At a time when Palestinians are facing genocide, occupation and forced displacement, attempts to silence those speaking out against Israel's actions are particularly alarming.

“Silencing Palestinian voices will not shut down the demand for justice and accountability.”

Students Stand AGAINST Sexual Violence (SSASV) is deeply disturbed by the actions of those in power this week and their attempts to silence activists.

We have seen a disgusting attack on protest rights in NSW yet again this week. On Tuesday night, we saw an egregious attempt to shut down Rising Tide’s “Paddle for the Planet”, a one-day, family-friendly flotilla at the world’s largest coal port to demand new jobs and funding for coal workers and a safe, liveable climate for everyone.

In an attempt to censor this action, Newcastle City Council’s Lord Mayor presented and passed a repressive motion prepared in secret collaboration with NSW Premier Minns and Police Minister Catley, which stated “that Council: Does not license or authorise, now and into the future, community-owned land for the purpose of Rising Tide’s events/protests (including, but not limited to, The People’s Blockade) and including its associates, subsidiaries, affiliated IMGs [issue motivated groups] and individuals.”

SSASV is UTTERLY DISGUSTED by this unprecedented attack on the right to protest.

Newcastle City Council has now banned approval of ANY EVENT OR PROTEST organised by Rising Tide or any associated groups on council-owned land “now and into the future”, leaving it unclear as to who can organise events on PUBLIC LAND in Newcastle.

Rising Tide has stated: “This is an attack on democratic participation, and follows in the footsteps of governments across the country restricting the right to protest,” which SSASV wholeheartedly agrees with.

The right to protest is absolutely crucial to the public's ability to be heard and participate in a democratic society.

A THREAT TO ONE IS A THREAT TO ALL.

SSASV stands in solidarity with the Rising Tide team and encourages you to sign and share their petition calling on the Lord Mayor and Newcastle City Council to unwind the ban on Rising Tide and affiliated groups.

We reject Newcastle Council’s authoritarian attempt to protect coal.

Last night, Newcastle Council passed a motion permanently banning Rising Tide, and any group or person associated with them, from using public land.

Many Trans Justice Project members, for example, would likely be banned from using public land.

This motion was prepared with support from NSW Premier Chris Minns and police minister Yasmin Catley.

Our government is attempting to crush democracy and control public life to defend the coal industry — which contributes to global warming that will kill billions.

We urge you to sign the petition demanding Newcastle Council drops this law, and to attend the upcoming Paddle for the Planet in Newcastle on November 14.

author: John Mullen
title: France: The brass band and the revolution
content:
For the third time in a week, there were major strikes in education and mass demonstrations across France, on November 10.

More than a million people took to the streets in more than 200 towns and cities, on November 5, in support of school students and to demand wage rises, more jobs and an end to cuts in public service budgets. Health workers, dockers, teachers, journalists, municipal staff, train drivers, bank workers and many others joined the one-day strike.

Two days later, hundreds of thousands marched again.

Student assemblies attracted more than a thousand participants at many universities, including Marseille, Rennes, Bordeaux and Paris-Cité.

In some towns, notably Rennes and Bordeaux, and in sectors such as university staff and healthcare, general assemblies of workers (known as interpros or coordinations) are taking the lead in organising the struggle, hoping to overcome the horrific inertia of the national union leaderships.

High school student representatives walked out of a government consultation session on university admissions policy, held in Paris on Monday November 9, when they discovered that ministers had invited fascist MPs to take part.

There are three strands to the present revolt.

First, highschool and university students are in their sixth week of blockades, and are not giving up despite the police beating thousands and mutilating dozens.

Secondly, the Yellow Vest networks are back, and they worry the government because they seem leaderless and prefer wildcat demos.

Most importantly, there is the workers’ movement, which holds, in strike action, our most powerful weapon, but which is held back by catastrophic national leadership from a band of professional “Bordeaux and sandwiches” negotiators.

On the demonstrations, people wave thousands upon thousands of home-made cardboard placards, with slogans from the bawdy to the philosophical, quoting poets, rappers or constitutional documents.

My favourites include: “Let’s do a poo on the fascists!”, “You thirst for power, we thirst for beauty!”, “Class struggle begins in high school!”, “Looters in hoodies make you angry? Looters in suits are your government !”, “Plan A: protest in a dignified manner. Plan B: smash everything up.”, “Have you forgotten how we became a democracy?” and “This is getting expensive in cardboard!”.

The now traditional demo song rings out across the country: “For the honour of the workers, and to build a better world! Although Macron doesn’t like it, here we are!”

Brass bands and orchestras are present everywhere, following a call from the New World Orchestra, who were tear-gassed while playing in mid-October. They have popularised a new demo song: “I’ve two great loves: the brass band and the revolution! Long live blockades and sabotage, occupations and wildcat demos!” Groups of thousands were filmed singing this and dancing.

Last week, a new opinion poll found that 57% of the population approves of the movement, and 88% consider the demands concerning purchasing power and the cost of living legitimate, while 75% approve of the students’ demands. This is impressive, given the massive government propaganda campaign against the revolt.

With such support, even the mainstream media feel obliged to feature interviews with inspiring high schoolers, explaining their demands in detail, even if the channels rapidly return to their preferred fare — interviews with headmasters, police and shopkeepers upset by the movement, and political experts who want to discuss supposed personality clashes between left politicians.

This crisis is not going to go away. Emmanuel Macron’s minority government must push its national budget through before Christmas. Massive tax cuts for the rich mean they are short of money, so their initial proposal is for €50 billion in budget cuts. The international bankers are breathing down their necks, already charging France more than neighbouring countries to borrow money.

The situation is extremely fluid. The government met with unions and bosses on November 9, and then declared that the national minimum monthly wage would be raised — by €24. The CGT union demand is for a €150 rise. Later this week a decision will be announced about public sector wages. Public servants have lost 20% of their purchasing power since 2010, and nearly a million are on the minimum wage.

The national union leaders are following their habitual hymn sheet of “days of action”. The dynamism of Thursday’s social explosion should have convinced them to call more action immediately, but they waited “to see the results of the negotiation”, which were, of course, pathetic.

Monday’s talks with the unions took place behind closed doors — they should have been live streamed. We could do with rallies outside the weekly meetings of the leaders of the six different union confederations, to help them concentrate.

Not all the union leaders are identical. The more radical, like Sophie Binet of the CGT confederation, say they would like to see strikes spread further, while the CFDT is not calling for more strikes right now. But all generally move very slowly, in practice.

The movements are enthusiastically supported by the radical left organisation La France Insoumise (France in Revolt). The result has been that FI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélénchon has gained a couple of percent in the opinion polls. It is unheard of to have such a huge movement within a few months of presidential elections, and the stakes are very high indeed. More mass strikes have been called by some union leaders for the 17th. We need to go further.

[John Mullen is a revolutionary socialist living in the Paris region and a supporter of the France Insoumise.]

title: Seven things you must never say about COP31
content:
COP31 opened in Antalya on November 9 and its two hosts — Türkiye and Australia — have been busy.

Australia’s Labor government, despite being elected on promises to act for the climate, has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

Since September 2025 it has signed 19 fossil fuel agreements: 20-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) contracts, oil and gas exploration pacts with ExxonMobil, Chevron and TotalEnergies, drilling rights from Syria to Somalia, and a deal with Australia’s Woodside.

On top of those come six nuclear and mining agreements, three of them were signed in Seoul on November 3, six days before the summit opened.

One host approves the projects. The other signs the contracts. Together they will run a summit whose Action Agenda does not name coal, oil or gas even once.

Everything is going smoothly. In Türkiye, censorship helps; at least 1270 X accounts were blocked in September alone and, over the past 20 months, trustees have been appointed to 10 television channels.

So, to keep the hosts comfortable, here are seven things you must never talk about.

1. Don’t talk about fossil philanthropy

In June, the foundations of the companies that change Türkiye’s climate the most, including a refinery, car factory, coal power plant, an electricity distributor and even the operator of Antalya airport, set up “Philanthropy for Climate”. They invited environmental groups to the table. The polluters bring the money; civil society brings the legitimacy. Australians who have watched gas companies sponsor festivals and sport will know the model.

2. Don’t talk about the COP31 bill

COP31 is expected to cost close to US$2 billion. When the host agreement came before Türkiye's parliament in July, one party wrote a dissenting opinion and then abstained. Only five MPs voted “No”. An agreement that cost to the public up to US$2 billion bill passed in near silence.

COP31 is, in a sense, a rubbish summit; “Zero waste” heads its list of themes. In August, as rubbish washed up along the Mediterranean coast, the national debate was only about waste imported from Britain. Meanwhile, according to Türkiye’s statistics office, more than 10 million tonnes of waste was burned in 2024. The sky became the landfill.

4. Don't talk about the fossil deals

Has anyone at COP31 mentioned the deals Türkiye signed while preparing to host it? The energy minister posed for photos at every ceremony. A 20-year LNG contract with Mercuria. Exploration in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean with ExxonMobil and TotalEnergies. A global partnership with Chevron, from Iraq to Venezuela. A stake in Kirkuk’s oil fields. Rights to drill in Syria, Libya, Somalia and Pakistan. And Woodside’s LNG.

When I counted in October, there were 14. Now there are 19.

5. Don’t talk about cities without resilience

On October 14, Istanbul, Sakarya, Kocaeli, Yalova, Muğla and Antalya went under water on the same day. The minister of urbanisation, who is also COP31 president, called it a “disaster”, blamed climate change and moved the topic onto the summit’s “Resilient Cities” theme. Were these resilient cities or cities stripped of their resilience? Between 2002 and 2021, Türkiye laid 603 million tonnes of asphalt and poured close to a billion tonnes of cement. If you must, talk only about river beds and pretend the valley slopes above them were never paved. In three days, everyone forgets.

6. Say ‘conference’, not ‘fair’

COP stands for Conference of the Parties. But it has become a Fair of the Parties. The minister announced that 1.5 million visitors are expected! That is not a venue for negotiation; it is an exhibition ground. As I argued last month, the stands will be busy and the products green. Never call it a fair. Say “climate summit”, a phrase with no actor and no action.

Say “coal phase-out”, but never mention oil. Ask for a coal exit date, which buys the government time. Don’t touch the summit’s global business partner, Koç Holding, which owns Türkiye's oil refineries. Call gas a “bridge fuel”. Australians know this one: Labor’s Future Gas Strategy says gas will be needed to 2050 and beyond.

So here are the seven things we must not talk about: Fossil philanthropy, the public bill, a country turned into a dump, fossil deals, asphalt-and-concrete cities, a summit turned trade fair, and oil and gas.

Nobody has to ban any of this, because we already don’t talk about it. We don't talk about the groups that sit at the table with fossil foundations. We don’t talk about asphalt and concrete, because their owners would come next.

We write reports about the changing climate, not about those who change it.

In Antalya there will be plenty of talk about “climate change”, with no subject and no verb. There will be no talk of 37 approvals in Canberra and 19 signatures in Ankara. No talk of three fossil fuels and two fossil infrastructures: coal, oil, gas, asphalt and concrete. Because if anyone talked about them, the conversation would arrive at the one policy both hosts share: the fossil order.

So, talk about it. In Sydney, in the Pacific and in Antalya. Thirty-seven and 19 new or expanded fossil fuel projects. Count them out loud.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim.]

title: Mascot residents organise against hyperscale AI data centre construction
content:
A community group has come together to oppose the Project Duke hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) data centre planned for Kent Street, Mascot.

Mascot Against AI Datacentres (MAAD) is organising to stop the project, which was approved by the NSW Department of Planning in December last year.

The 90–120 megawatt project was approved under State Significant Development rules that bypass local council approval processes. It would join data centres in nearby Alexandria and Roseberry, including an 18MW data centre on Gardeners Road and an 84MW data centre on Bourke Road.

The processing power required for AI means that these data centres use significantly more energy and water than regular data centres.

Project Duke is the largest approved AI data centre near the CBD. It is set to consume enough energy for 64,000 households and will use as much water a day as 30,000 people. It will also produce constant noise that will impact nearby apartment buildings.

It will feature diesel generators and above ground diesel tanks that can store up to 783,000 liters. While diesel generators are pitched as emergency only reserves, in case of power shortages, some data centres reportedly use diesel generators on a regular basis.

title: NSW Police take Rising Tide to Supreme Court over Newcastle Harbour paddle out protest
content:

NSW Police has taken RT to court for previous protests in Newcastle Harbour, and have carried out mass arrests of protesters, most of whom have had their charges dropped.

title: Qld LNP crushes public sector workers’ right to organise
content:
The Queensland Liberal National Party (LNP) government introduced legislation in October to make it more difficult for state public sector and local council workers to organise and take industrial action. Nearly 400,000 workers in the state who are not covered by the federal Fair Work Act will be impacted.

The legislation raises the threshold for workers’ compensation claims for psychological injury, requiring work to be the “major significant” cause of the injury. This could reduce the number of claims for these injuries, about which workers are now more conscious.

It does not address these injuries’ causes, such as the unsafe conditions, excessive workloads, chronic understaffing and exposure to violence and abuse faced by public sector workers, who are five times more likely than other workers to experience psychological injury, according to Queensland Unions (QU).

The legislation introduces the restrictive provisions already included in federal laws that make it more difficult for workers to take industrial action. This includes restrictions on union organisers' right to enter workplaces with “fit and proper person” tests, a requirement of three working days’ notice before taking industrial action and allowing employers to reduce pay during industrial action partial bans and withhold pay from workers on strike.

author: John Mullen
title: Update from France: Towards an explosive general strike?
content:
The sharp upturn in class struggle continues in France, with school students and workers demanding more for ordinary people and far less for bankers and billionaires.

The Emmanuel Macron government is setting up ever more authoritarian institutions and practices, demanding harsh sentences for those arrested, and mutilating teenagers, while making minor concessions. The trade union leaderships are calling, mostly half-heartedly, for mass strike action this week. An explosion is possible.

The hundreds of demonstrations on October 24 and 31 were a major victory for the movement. The government's attempt to scare people off the streets failed. Despite bans and curfews and a solemn presidential speech ("we recommend that people do not demonstrate"), despite invented figures about injured cops and the cost of damage to public buildings, the movement is going forward.

Many were too frightened to go to these protests (two more people were mutilated by cops on the 24th), but more turned up, in an atmosphere of joyous revolt. Support is flooding in from very varied places: the magistrates' union, for example, has denounced the "brutality" of police action, a group of Catholic activists published an open letter to their right-wing bishops entitled "We are proud to take part in the uprising", and the Louvre museum was blockaded last week by Fine Arts students.

The repression was ratcheted up. For the 31st, demonstrations were banned in many city centres and peripheral routes were imposed. More than 100 towns and cities have been affected by curfews or restrictions on assembly.

This week, using the excuse of the rioting in mid-October, Macron is trying to push through parliament a new law. It increases penalties for looting, but would also impose heavy punishment for refusing to leave a demonstration when the police tell you to; it would give police the power to ban individuals from attending protests for up to three years, and allow the authorities to confiscate wages or social benefits of people "present in an assembly" where looting takes place (even if the individuals involved are not accused of any offence).

The far right, which hopes to win the presidency next May, applauds every new repressive measure.

The government seems to make additional minor concessions each week. We have seen 3000 replacement teachers hired, smaller classes (of 28 pupils) announced for 15-year-olds, 15,000 more student places promised in higher education, small increases in grants for poorer students, and more loans for regional governments to rebuild crumbling high schools.

This week Macron announced "a complete remoulding" of the hated Parcoursup platform, which controls who gets into which university … in 2028, long after the next elections! Some concessions answer student demands directly, but far more is needed.

Working-class combativity has long protected some aspects of French education from neoliberalism: enrolling in university costs less than €300 a year, for example. But this movement is not a defensive one. It is demanding more: 250,000 more places in higher education and €5 billion for school buildings, for a start.

As high schools and universities finished their autumn break on November 2, there was little sign of calm. A regional university student coordinating meeting, with representatives from a dozen universities, met for the second time on October 31: just one example of the important grassroots initiatives building the revolt.

That same day, almost all docks in France were closed as workers struck both against war and against proposed cuts in welfare being discussed in parliament. Their demands include an increase in the minimum wage for all workers.

As I write, the general strike for November 5 is being prepared, in support of the high schools and for increases in wages and hirings. It will be huge.

After a delay by union leaderships — which it is difficult not to describe as criminal — one month after the beginning of the movement, mass strike action has finally been called across the economy by five of the six biggest union confederations.

One of the biggest, the General Confederation of Workers (CGT), is asking strikers to organise workplace meetings and to "generalise the strike on the 5th November and afterwards". (The "renewable strike", re-voted in general meetings every couple of days, is an excellent tradition in the French workers' movement, but it can also be used as an excuse by leaderships to avoid organising stronger action themselves.)

This mix — of a long young people’s revolt the government will not satisfy, rising anger among workers about the cost of living, and a budget being prepared by Macron ‘s government this month aiming at slashing tens of billions of euros from public spending — may be explosive.

In the public sector in France less than 20% of workers are members of a union, and in the private sector less than 10%. One reason for these low figures is that many benefits of union influence are available to non-members. Millions of non-members nevertheless vote for, and are represented by, union candidates for health and safety committees, company councils, industrial tribunals, regional and sectoral wages councils, and other such bodies. Agreements signed by trade unions generally apply to all workers.

The right to strike is part of the French constitution, and non-union workers are legally fairly well protected by the strike declarations made by unions. This relatively solid legal protection means it is very common, on days of action, to have minorities in a workplace taking strike action. One school or bus depot might have 20% on strike, another 80%.

A key historical weakness of the union movement here is its division into six — sometimes competing — confederations. In some sectors, workers tend to just join the biggest union in their workplace. Frequently, though, people choose the union according to their politics. The CGT (which used to be extremely close to the Communist Party) is generally more combative than the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT). Solidaires (Solidarity) is the most combative and the most left-wing, and less politicised workers don't generally join it.

The bosses and the government can play the federations off against each other, and the union leaders from the more combative confederations can and do use the excuse that "the others weren't ready to fight" to give up the struggle quickly themselves.

National union leaders in France do not receive the exorbitant salaries their counterparts in countries like Britain do, but they are still professional negotiators, and have a strong interest in movements not exploding out of their control.

During the movement to defend pensions in 2023, the big unions called at least 11 one-day strikes, generally a week or two apart. After each day of action, all six confederations met behind closed doors to decide what to do next, and always agreed to move at the pace of the slowest. The result was that the movement did not achieve its aims. There should have been mass rallies in front of the building during each of those meetings!

Rank-and-file workers may vote on the 5th to extend the strike, and this is the main hope for an escalation. But those who say the union leaders should be completely ignored are mistake. We pay their wages, they have mass influence, and we should demand loudly that they lead a general strike. There is easily enough support in the country to make this a realistic option. The government is rattled, so much so that this week they are talking about raising the national minimum wage (by a little). After the May 1968 revolt, with 10 million on strike, the minimum wage was raised by 35%, so the best strategy is not hard to work out.

The upcoming presidential election is on everyone's mind, especially as polling suggests a second-round showdown between fascist Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical-left France Insoumise (FI). Placards supporting Mélenchon are a common sight among protesters; FI MPs are actively backing the movement and opposing police violence, drawing loud applause at demonstrations. Meanwhile, right-wing presidential hopeful Bruno Retailleau has gone so far as to call for the organisation to be banned.

What happens over the next couple of weeks will heavily shape the broader political landscape and the elections ahead. Escalation is needed now.

[John Mullen is a revolutionary socialist living in the Paris region, and a supporter of the France Insoumise. His website is randombolshevik.org.]

author: John Tully
title: Australia can build public housing, end homelessness
content:
I often walk my dog in Nipaluna/Hobart’s beautiful Rivulet Linear Park, which winds up from the city to the foothills of Mount Wellington. If you’re lucky, you can spot a platypus in the rivulet, there are flocks of gorgeously plumed parrots, and the marsupial population is thriving.

But that’s not all you’ll see, for half-hidden in the bushes there are tent encampments: places of last resort for some of Lutruwita/Tasmania’s homeless people. Others huddle on pieces of cardboard in shop doorways in the CBD or in other parks.

Sleeping rough exposes people to the vagaries of the elements, the threat of theft and violence and a constant battle to maintain good health and sanitation.

A fine line now separates countless numbers of working-class people from a similar fate. With the country’s median rents at $705 per week — an increase of 40.6% in the past five years — half of all people who live in rental accommodation are struggling to put food on the table and pay rent and other bills.

About 45% of families with children struggle to buy sufficient food — an estimated 3.6 million people, 69% of whom report they are facing food insecurity for the first time.

The link between the cost-of-living crisis and soaring rents is clear: 1.26 million households are forced to pay more than 30% of their disposable income on rent, which doesn’t leave much for food, utilities, education and medical care.

This crisis disproportionately impacts renters — though this is not to downplay the struggles of many to pay their mortgages with rising interest rates.

Unforeseen bills can send renters into a downward spiral of debt and homelessness. Elderly and middle-aged women, often with little savings to fall back on, can find themselves out on the street.

About 48% of 18–34-year-olds find themselves in precarious living circumstances.

While the United States/Israeli war on Iran turbocharged the cost-of-living crisis by forcing up the price of fuel and fertilisers, this conjunctural crisis only added to the existing pressures in a country where millions of people are priced out of home ownership and are reliant on the private rental market.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Australia is the third wealthiest country in terms of median wealth, and the fifth wealthiest in terms of average wealth.

However this wealth is not distributed evenly. The top 1% are wealthier than the bottom 50$ combined, and much of their wealth is in property and real estate.

With Labor, the Coalition and One Nation pushing politics further to the right, there is little challenge to the neoliberal dogmas that had led us to this crisis.

Those three parties are firmly wedded to the private rental market. Indeed, many politicians have a personal interest in maintaining it.

According to the Guardian, at least 55% of federal politicians own multiple properties, and between 50 to 92 are actively receiving rental income.

Meanwhile, public housing has declined to only 4% of housing stock.

This is an ideological choice with disastrous consequences. While Australia does better than the US, where less than 1% of households live in any form of social or public housing, we compare poorly with most OECD countries.

Countries like the Netherlands (29%), Austria (24%), Denmark (21%), Sweden (17%) and Britain (17%) have far greater percentages of public housing stock than Australia. In Vienna, and other city centres that have consciously prioritised public housing, that figure can rise to more than 50%.

Social housing is nothing new — at least to those who care to look.

I recently visited the oldest public housing project in the world, the Fuggerei, in the southern German city of Augsburg, founded in 1521. The project’s museum points out that “people have continuously been living in the Fuggerei for half a millennium”.

One of the early residents was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s great-grandfather, the impoverished bricklayer, Franz Mozart. “When the project’s major donor, the banker Jakob Fugger, died in 1525, there were 52 houses in the complex. Today, the Fuggerei consists of 140 flats in 67 houses, with other buildings for administration, a museum and workshops.”

The Fuggerei is not a ghetto of poverty and despair. It is a beautiful place, with homes meeting modern living standards with heating, modern bathrooms, television and the internet.

It has some strict conditions for residence, designed for “Catholic Augsburg residents in need”, who must contribute three prayers a day and 88 euro cents in annual rent.

If such a project could be built and maintained for more than 500 years, why is it that a wealthy country like Australia fares so poorly?

Safe, secure, affordable and well-maintained housing should be regarded as a human right, not as a cash cow for wealthy landlords.

title: Forum discusses corruption and inhumanity in offshore detention regime
content:
